name: PT Indo Kordsa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indo Kordsa: half of book for a recovering tyre-cord franchise
frontmatter.summary: Indo Kordsa, the Indonesian tyre-cord arm of Turkey's Kordsa, trades at 0.5x book after a flood-hit year. H1 2026 shows the operating recovery is real, and our DCF values the equity at Rp7,850 a share. After scenario weighting and the liquidity discount the target is Rp6,014 (BUY, 34.6% expected return). The related-party loan and investment property are the swing factors.
thesis: The market treats the flood year as the new normal: at 4.7x FY2026E EBITDA and 0.5x book, the shares embed no recovery, while H1 2026 delivered gross profit of US$13.7m and operating profit of US$10.4m [S2][S3].

Capacity is under-used, not obsolete: TCF output of 24,606 mt against 60 kt of fabric capacity leaves operating leverage as Indonesian tyre production follows the 760,476-unit ten-month car market [S4][S8].
The balance sheet carries a US$40.0m related-party loan and US$15.1m of investment property at book, both outside the operating DCF and both largely ignored by the market capitalisation [S2].
Liquidity is the discount: ADTV of IDR6.0m earns a 30% haircut, which is why the target sits below our fundamental value [S0].

catalysts.event: Q3 2026 LK; TCF volume, gross margin and export mix
FY2026 audited results and dividend proposal
Monthly Gaikindo wholesale and retail data

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Indo Kordsa at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp6,014, 34.6% above the Rp4,600 market price, plus a dividend yield that our forecast puts near 3.9% [S0][S7]. The shares are not cheap because the business is good; they are cheap because the market is still pricing the March 2025 flood as a lasting loss of earning power. At 4.7x our FY2026E EBITDA and 0.5x book, the operating business is valued at little more than its working capital [S0][S2].

The variant view is that the flood was a temporary interruption, not a structural break. The Citeureup plant restarted within months, the group booked a net flood charge of only US$1.9m in FY2025 after recovering US$21.5m of insurance, and H1 2026 revenue reached US$83.0m against TCF sales volume of 22,793 mt in the whole of FY2025 and 60 kt of capacity [S2][S3][S4]. The first half also produced operating profit of US$10.4m, of which US$5.0m was one-off flood income; even stripping that out, the underlying operating result is a clear recovery from the prior year [S2]. Our base case takes revenue back to the FY2024 level by FY2030, because the capacity to do so was never lost [S3][S4].

Three things move the value. First, TCF utilisation: at 22,793 mt of sales volume in FY2025 against 60 kt of capacity, every incremental tonne carries a high contribution margin [S4]. Second, the non-operating assets: the US$40.0m loan to the parent and the US$15.1m investment property are carried at book in our bridge and together exceed a quarter of the market capitalisation [S2][S0]. Third, liquidity: with ADTV of IDR6.0m, the shares attract a 30% discount in the target, and that discount, not the fundamental value, is the main reason the rating is BUY rather than a stronger call [S0].

The case fails if Indonesian tyre production does not follow the car-market recovery, if Chinese tyre brands take enough domestic share to force cord-price concessions, or if the related-party loan is repaid on terms that destroy the interest income [S8][S9]. We treat those as the bear case, not the base case, and we show the arithmetic in the risk section. One qualification runs through the whole report: the cash-flow record is partly an insurance settlement, and receivables have grown much faster than revenue, so the earnings quality is good but not as clean as the headline cash conversion suggests [S2][S3].

PT Indo Kordsa makes the reinforcement that goes into tyres. Its product set is tire cord fabric (TCF), nylon yarn and polyester HMLS yarn; the fabric is woven from the yarn and processed into dipped cord fabric that tyre makers calender into the carcass and belt packages [S4]. The company is not a tyre maker and does not sell to car buyers directly: its customer is the tyre plant, so its volume driver is tyre production rather than car sales [S4][S3]. That distinction matters for how we read the Indonesian car market in the next section.

The operating footprint is the Citeureup complex in Bogor, West Java, plus Thai Indo Kordsa in Ayutthaya, Thailand [S4]. Capacity is 60 kt a year of fabric, 46 kt of polyester yarn and 24 kt of nylon yarn [S4]. FY2025 output was 24,606 mt of TCF, 8,450 mt of nylon and 24,551 mt of polyester; the TCF number was down because the flood stopped the plant, not because the capacity disappeared [S4][S3].

The revenue mix is concentrated in fabric. FY2025 TCF sales were US$107.1m, the large majority of group revenue; nylon contributed US$1.5m and polyester US$15.6m [S4]. Exports were US$56.3m of FY2025 revenue and local sales US$68.3m; in H1 2026 the split was almost even, with exports of US$41.2m and local sales of US$42.0m [S3][S2]. The Thai subsidiary sells into its own regional tyre plants, so the group has a second production base outside Indonesia [S4].

The customer base is the large tyre makers, and qualification is the moat. A new cord supplier has to pass compound, adhesion and endurance tests at each tyre plant, and requalification is slow; the company established the Asia Pacific Technical Centre in Citeureup as an innovation and development hub to co-develop new constructions with those customers [S4]. The revenue note states that no single customer accounts for more than a tenth of net revenue, which cuts single-name risk but also means the company has little pricing power against any one buyer [S2].

The controlling shareholder is Kordsa Teknik Tekstil A.S., part of Turkey's Sabanci Holding group, with 61.6% of the shares [S4]. The Indonesian listing dates from the Branta Mulia era; the company took the Kordsa name after the Turkish acquisition in 2006 and merged PT Indo Kordsa Polyester into the listed entity with effect from the start of 2023, which is why the share count is 450m [S4]. The group relationship brings technology and a regional production and distribution network, but it also brings the related-party transactions we examine in the governance section [S3].

Strategy is straightforward: run the existing asset base harder, lift the export mix, and move toward higher-value nylon and polyester constructions rather than add greenfield fabric capacity [S4]. The APAC Technical Centre and the polyester line are the main growth investments; the balance sheet is under-levered, so the constraint is demand, not capital [S2][S4].

Tyre cord fabric sits one step upstream of the tyre plant. Demand is driven by tyre production, which in turn follows vehicle production, replacement demand and tyre exports; car sales are a leading indicator of the replacement cycle, not a direct input [S4]. Indonesia is a large tyre-producing country, and the local tyre makers are both customers and competitors for the same regional export orders as other cord producers [S4][S9].

The car market has been strong. Gaikindo wholesales reached 760,476 units in the first ten months of 2026, up sharply on the same period a year earlier, and the article reports retail sales running at a similar level [S8]. That is a genuine tailwind for tyre production, and therefore for cord demand, but it is not a one-for-one translation: tyre makers run their own inventory cycles, and the export tyre market is separate from the domestic car market [S8][S4].

The competitive threat is Chinese tyre brands. Indonesian tyre retail is seeing a growing number of Chinese brands, and the incumbents are responding with price and distribution rather than capacity withdrawal [S9]. For a cord supplier that matters twice: Chinese tyre plants in Indonesia are potential customers, but they also pressure the pricing of the tyres that the established makers sell, which eventually feeds back into cord prices [S9][S3].

The pre-flood decline was a cord-price problem, not a volume problem, and that is the base rate for the terminal margin. Consolidated revenue fell from US$335.2m in FY2022 to US$252.0m in FY2023 and US$230.9m in FY2024, so roughly a third of the revenue base disappeared before the flood [S0]. The segment note shows where it went: external TCF sales fell from US$231.5m in FY2023 to US$194.8m in FY2024 while polyester external sales rose from US$14.8m to US$25.6m [S5]. TCF sales volume in FY2024 was still 45,766 mt against 60 kt of capacity, so the plant was running at around three-quarters of capacity while the cord price fell: the decline was price and mix, not lost volume [S4]. That is why we fade the gross margin to 16.0% rather than hold the H1 2026 level for ever, and why the bear case runs the margin back toward the FY2024 level [S3][S9].
The FY2025 gross margin of 8.5% was flood-depressed, but even the FY2024 level of 15.7% was below the FY2022 peak, which is the price trend the industry has to live with [S3].

On the five forces, buyer power is high: the tyre majors are large, qualified and able to dual-source, and the credit-risk note confirms a fragmented but professional buyer base [S3]. Supplier power is moderate: nylon and polyester chip prices track oil and caprolactam, and the company buys part of its raw material from related parties, which we treat as a governance rather than a cost issue [S3]. The threat of new entrants is low at the qualified-plant level because of the testing cycle, but high at the commodity-yarn level, especially from Chinese and Indian producers [S4][S9]. Substitute materials exist in specialty tyres but are not a volume threat in mass-market tyres [S4]. Rivalry is moderate and regional, with the Thai subsidiary competing inside the same group network [S4].

The moat is narrow, not wide. The qualification cycle and the technical centre give incumbency, and the Citeureup site has scale and infrastructure that would be expensive to replicate [S4]. But the product is a specified industrial input, not a branded consumer good, and the customer can move the specification to another qualified supplier when the price gap is large enough [S3][S9]. That is why we cross-check the business at a mid-single-digit EBITDA multiple and do not assume a permanent margin expansion [S3].

Tyre cord fabric is the woven reinforcement that gives a radial tyre its shape and load capacity. Nylon
is favoured in the carcass because it is tough and heat-resistant; polyester HMLS is used where
dimensional stability and low shrinkage matter. The cord is dipped in adhesive, calendered into rubber
and cut to the tyre-building line, so the supplier is tied into the tyre maker's engineering and
quality systems rather than selling a spot commodity.

External influences are the rupiah, oil-linked raw materials and trade policy. Revenue is invoiced mostly in US dollars on the export book, while a large part of the cost base is rupiah, so a weaker rupiah helps the export margin and hurts domestic purchasing power [S3][S2]. The export share is moving: H1 2026 had exports of US$41.2m against local sales of US$42.0m, close to half the book, against US$56.3m of export sales in the whole of FY2025 [S2][S3]. The house macro deck carries the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD against a spot of Rp18,103/USD, and that weaker path helps a dollar-revenue, rupiah-cost mix [S0]. The LK does not disclose a margin split between export and local sales, so we carry the mix shift through the revenue and gross-margin path rather than invent a separate export margin [S2]. Oil sets the direction of caprolactam and polyester chip costs, and the company has limited ability to pass through a sharp move within a quarter [S3]. Trade policy is a wildcard: anti-dumping actions or a change in the export destinations of Chinese tyre makers would redirect cord demand quickly, and we do not model a specific policy outcome [S9].

The last four years tell a clear story. Revenue fell from US$335.2m in FY2022 to US$252.0m, then US$230.9m, and then collapsed to US$124.3m when the flood stopped the Citeureup plant and TCF output fell [S0][S3][S4]. EBITDA followed the same path, from US$29.5m in FY2024 to US$10.8m in FY2025, and net profit to the parent turned negative at US$-2.3m [S3]. The H1 2026 rebound is the first clean read on the recovered asset: revenue of US$83.0m, gross profit of US$13.7m and operating profit of US$10.4m, including the one-off flood income [S2].

Our FY2026E revenue of US$165.3m, a 33.0% increase, is anchored on the H1 actual alone: H1 2026 revenue was US$83.0m against US$61.8m in H1 2025, and doubling the half-year would give a little more than we carry [S2]. The FY2025 base is so depressed that the growth rate flatters the recovery; the more useful comparison is that FY2026E revenue is still below FY2024 [S3]. We then grow revenue 18.0% in FY2027E, 10.0% in FY2028E and 6.0% in FY2029E, which carries the group past the FY2024 level of US$230.9m by FY2030 on a plant that still has the capacity [S4]. That is what a temporary interruption looks like in numbers, and it is the path we test in the bear case rather than assume [S3][S4].

Gross margin is the swing variable. H1 2026 gross margin was 16.5% in the model, built from the H1 actual [S2]. We hold that level through FY2028E and fade to 16.0% by FY2030E as Chinese tyre competition pressures cord pricing [S9]. We do not add a step for volume: H1 2026 already earned a higher margin than FY2024 on lower revenue, so the gain came from price and mix rather than fixed-cost absorption, and the absorption is taken once, below the gross line, in the falling opex ratio [S2][S3]. That is a recovery, not a return to the FY2022 peak: the FY2022 gross margin of 20.0% reflected a tighter cord market that we do not assume recurs [S3].

The cost base has two features the data pack gets wrong. First, D&A: the pack's depreciation line is an order of magnitude below the LK's total depreciation and amortisation, which was US$10.4m in FY2025 and US$10.7m in FY2024, roughly the fixed charge on a US$212.4m equity base and a large fixed-asset stock [S3]. We restate both years, which is why our EBITDA is higher than the pack's and why the EV/EBITDA cross-check uses a sensible denominator [S3]. Second, finance costs: the pack's interest line is only the interest sub-component, while total finance costs were US$0.7m in FY2025 and US$1.3m in FY2024 [S3]. The difference is other finance cost, mainly lease and facility charges, and we use the total for the cost-of-debt calibration [S3].

Operating costs are running at US$16.4m on revenue of US$165.3m, or 10.0% of sales: the H1 2026 selling and G&A lines were US$4.1m and US$3.3m, and we add the two lines the LK carries above operating profit, a currency exchange loss of US$0.3m and an other loss of US$0.5m [S2]. Both recur, since FY2025 and FY2024 also booked exchange losses, so leaving them out of the cost base would flatter EBITDA by about a percentage point of sales [S3][S2]. Export fees are the largest selling cost and scale with the export mix, which is why the ratio falls to 8.2% by FY2030E rather than to the FY2024 level at once [S2][S3]. The D&A ratio falls from 5.9% of revenue in FY2026E to 5.5% in FY2030E as revenue grows against a largely fixed asset base; H1 2026 ran at a lower ratio than the full-year FY2025 charge, so the direction is with the trend, not against it [S3][S2].

Cash conversion needs a qualification before it can be called a strength. Operating cash flow was US$25.4m in FY2025, ahead of a net loss, and US$23.1m in FY2024 [S3]. But the FY2025 figure includes US$11.5m of insurance claim cash, so ex-insurance it was below the prior year, and the H1 2026 operating cash flow of US$9.8m includes US$15.2m of insurance that turns the half into a small outflow before the claim [S3][S2]. Capex was US$13.4m in FY2025, including the flood rebuild, and we model US$9.1m in FY2026E, at or above the D&A charge from FY2027E so that the asset base is maintained rather than run down [S2][S3]. Free cash flow to the firm was negative in FY2025 because of the flood and the working-capital build, but turns positive at US$12.9m in FY2026E [S3]. Working capital is US$41.3m, or 25.0% of revenue, in line with the June 2026 trade working-capital position [S2].

The balance sheet is conservative. At end-FY2025 the company held US$21.7m of cash against US$2.6m of debt, and the June 2026 position is similar [S3][S2]. Debt is small relative to cash and to the asset base, so refinancing risk is not material [S3]. The equity base is US$212.4m, which at the current share count is a book value per share well above the market price [S0][S3].

Capital allocation is dividend-first. The FY2025 dividend was IDR200 per share, or IDR90,011m in total, paid from retained earnings even though the year was a loss [S7]. We found no buyback in the cash-flow statement, and the only material investing outflow beyond capex was the related-party loan [S2][S3]. We model a 45.0% payout, which keeps the dividend near the level the board has actually paid while retaining enough cash to fund the rebuild [S7][S2].

Earnings quality is mixed rather than clean. The accruals screen passes on the reported numbers, because operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2025 and FY2024, but strip the insurance receipts and the working-capital build does much of the work [S3][S2]. Two optics-class flags need naming. Inventory rose to US$35.6m at 30 June 2026 from US$30.6m at December as the plant restarted and the company rebuilt stock [S2][S3]. Trade receivables rose to US$36.5m at 30 June 2026 from US$22.2m at December and US$15.7m a year earlier, while revenue rose far less, so days sales outstanding roughly doubled year on year: that is the receivables-divergence test in our earnings-quality card firing [S2][S6][S3]. The related-party share of that receivable is US$9.1m, up by more than half since December, so part of the build is trade with the controlling group rather than with independent tyre makers [S2]. None of this looks like fabrication: the balances are disclosed, the customers are real and the cash arrives with a lag. But we do not give cash conversion the benefit of the doubt, our working-capital ratio holds the June level rather than assuming a release, and the FY2025 tax charge is not a useful run-rate because it was struck on a near-zero pretax base; H1 2026's US$2.9m of tax on US$12.0m of pretax profit is the cleaner guide, and we use a 24.0% rate [S2][S3].

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and P/BV as cross-checks. That set fits an asset-heavy, cyclical industrial with a single reporting currency and a depressed earnings base: P/E is unusable while trailing earnings are negative, EV/EBITDA is the sector's normal yardstick but needs a trough-year caveat, and P/BV tests the central claim directly because the shares trade below book [S3][S2]. The engine therefore drops P/E and weights DCF at 71%, EV/EBITDA at 14% and P/BV at 14% [S3].

The cost of capital is the usual Indonesia build. The risk-free rate is 4.86%, the mature-market equity premium 4.23%, the Indonesia country premium 2.46%, and the industry unlevered beta 0.90, giving a levered beta of 0.92 at a 0.02 debt-to-equity ratio [S3]. The cost of equity is 10.98% and the WACC 10.86%, with debt costing 6.86% pre-tax and a 22% tax rate [S3].

The USD-reporting-currency point needs a word. The engine runs the model in US dollars because the company reports in US dollars, but the cash flows are generated in Indonesia and a large part of the cost base is rupiah. Applying the Indonesia country premium to a USD risk-free rate therefore produces a rate that is the USD equivalent of an IDR cost of equity, not a rate for a US-dollar business with US-dollar costs. At 10.98% it sits just below the floor of the IDR band we use for industrial names and above the pure USD band; it is the correct rate for these cash flows and we do not add a second country premium, but it is the bottom of the range, and the reason is leverage rather than a kinder view of the risk [S3][S2]. Debt is 2.1% of the capital structure, so the levered beta of 0.92 is barely above the industry's unlevered 0.90; peers carrying real debt run a higher cost of equity on the same asset beta [S3]. A reader who wants a premium for the thin liquidity will find it in the target's 30% haircut, not in the discount rate.

The house macro deck, not only the company, sets the backdrop. The regime held through this cycle is balance-of-payments pressure on the cautious setting, and the sector stance is AVOID on Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer discretionary [S0]. BRAM sits in that sector but not of it: revenue is dollar-invoiced (exports were US$56.3m of FY2025 sales) and the balance sheet is in net cash, so the rate and currency channel that drives the AVOID stance reaches the company through its customers' volumes rather than through its own funding cost [S2][S3]. We convert the dollar DCF at the deck spot of Rp18,103/USD rather than the FY2027E rate of Rp18,350/USD, because the target is a twelve-month price and spot is the rate an investor deals at today; at the deck's forward rate the rupiah target would translate a little higher, and the deck's weaker-rupiah path is a modest tailwind to the export margin in the forecast [S0][S2].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of US$128.9m and a value of Rp7,850 per share after net cash, minorities and the bridge [S3][S2]. The terminal value is 51.0% of enterprise value, so the explicit forecast and the terminal value carry roughly equal weight; that split is normal for a company with a long-lived, maintainable asset base and a five-year explicit window, and we have kept terminal capex at or above D&A so the terminal value is not flattered by a shrinking asset base [S3]. The terminal growth of 2.5% is the USD cap [S3]. We do not use a life-of-asset DCF because the plant has no disclosed reserve life and the assets are maintainable indefinitely with normal capex [S4].

The bridge is where the non-operating value sits. The company holds US$21.7m of cash against US$2.6m of debt, plus a US$40.0m working-capital loan to Kordsa Teknik Tekstil A.S. bearing interest at six-month SOFR plus a margin, and US$15.1m of investment property at carrying value [S2][S3]. The loan is a financial asset, not an operating asset: its interest income sits in other non-operating income and is taxed in the model, and the principal is added at book in the bridge [S2]. The property is carried separately from PPE and is likewise added at book; we do not model rental income, which is conservative [S2]. Together the two items add US$40.0m plus US$15.1m to equity value, and they are the reason the DCF equity value is above the enterprise value [S2].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check lands at Rp5,190 a share, using a 5.8x multiple on LTM EBITDA of US$10.8m and the same bridge [S3]. That denominator is the flood year, since EBITDA was US$10.8m against US$20.6m in our FY2026E, so on this company the method is structurally too low; we have therefore cut its weight to 14% rather than let a trough multiple pull the blend away from a DCF that capitalises a normal year [S3][S2]. Read on FY2026E EBITDA the same multiple would be worth materially more, and the market is paying 4.7x for that EBITDA today [S2]. The -33.9% gap to the DCF measures the flood-year distortion, not a disagreement about the business. Both the DCF and the multiple are struck on an enterprise value of market capitalisation plus net debt and minorities, with the related-party loan and the investment property left outside as bridge items, so the two are on the same definition and the reader is not comparing apples with pears [S2][S3].

The P/BV cross-check lands at Rp7,563 a share on a 0.9x multiple of the US$212.4m equity base, close to the DCF and therefore the strongest independent support for the thesis [S2][S3]. It is also the cleanest test of the "half of book" argument in the summary: a multiple near one times book is not a demanding assumption for a business earning a positive return on equity in a normal year, and the value only fails if the equity base itself is impaired - which is why the related-party receivable and the loan are governance questions rather than footnotes [S2][S3].

The sensitivity is wide, as it should be for a cyclical. At a WACC one percentage point higher and terminal growth a point lower, the DCF value falls to the bottom of the grid; at the opposite corner it rises above Rp7,850 [S3]. The gross-margin sensitivity is the more useful one for a reader: a two-percentage-point margin miss takes a large slice of the value, which is why we treat the Chinese-tyre price pressure as the key risk rather than a footnote [S9].

The target construction is deliberately mechanical. The method blend gives Rp7,429 today; rolling that forward one year at the cost of equity and subtracting the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp177 gives the base-scenario value of Rp8,067. Probability-weighting the bear, base and bull scenarios gives Rp8,592, and applying the 30% liquidity discount gives the target of Rp6,014 [S0][S3]. The discount is not a judgment about the business; it is the house rule for a stock with ADTV of IDR6.0m and a free float of 16.0% [S0].

The reverse DCF returns no solution: the engine reports that the market price is not bracketed by its growth search range, so we do not publish an implied growth rate. What the levels say is plain. At Rp4,600 the market capitalisation is IDR2,070,262,108.00tn, while the DCF's enterprise value is US$128.9m and the non-operating items add a further US$40.0m plus US$15.1m [S0][S2][S3]. Converted at the spot rate of 18,103 rupiah to the dollar, the balance-sheet items alone account for a substantial share of the market capitalisation, so the price is discounting a deep and lasting contraction of the operating business. We report that as a signal about how little the market is paying for the operating franchise, not as a valuation output [S0][S2].

The risks that matter are operational, competitive, governance and liquidity, in that order. Macro and FX are real but second-order for a company with net cash and dollar revenue; the balance sheet can absorb a cyclical downturn without a refinancing [S3][S2].

The first risk is operational: another flood or a long plant outage. The Citeureup site flooded in March 2025, the group booked gross losses of US$23.4m and recovered US$21.5m of insurance, and the net charge was US$1.9m [S3]. The company has since rebuilt the plant and collected the insurance recovery, but the site is in a flood-prone area and a repeat event would hit output and cash flow at the same time [S3][S4]. Likelihood is moderate over a multi-year horizon; impact is high in the year of the event but manageable thereafter because the balance sheet is net cash [S2].

The second risk is competitive: Chinese tyre brands taking domestic share and forcing cord-price concessions. The trade press reports a growing Chinese tyre presence in Indonesia, and the incumbents are responding on price [S9]. If the tyre makers cannot hold price, they will push the adjustment up the chain to cord suppliers, and the FY2024 gross margin of 15.7% is a better guide to the downside than the FY2022 peak [S3][S9]. Likelihood is moderate-to-high; impact is a lower terminal margin and a lower multiple, which is what our bear case captures [S3].

The third risk is governance and related parties. Kordsa owns 61.6% of the shares; 12.1% of FY2025 sales and 20.2% of inventory purchases were with related parties, the company has a US$40.0m loan receivable from the parent, and related-party trade receivables were US$9.1m at 30 June 2026, up by more than half since December [S3][S2]. The loan is disclosed, priced at a market-based rate and approved through the usual process, but it ties up a large slice of the balance sheet with the controlling shareholder, and a repayment or a change in terms would remove the interest income we carry in other non-operating income [S2]. Likelihood of a value-destructive related-party action is low given the disclosure and the audit committee, but the governance discount is real; it is part of why the stock trades below book [S3].

The fourth risk is liquidity. ADTV of IDR6.0m and a free float of 16.0% mean an institutional position cannot be built or exited quickly, and the target already carries a 30% discount [S0]. A further shrinking of the free float, or an index change, would widen that discount rather than narrow it [S0].

The macro and FX risks are milder. Revenue is largely dollar-denominated, costs are mixed, and the company has net cash, so a rupiah depreciation is a margin tailwind rather than a solvency risk [S2][S3]. A rise in Indonesian rates raises the cost of equity and the discount rate, but the debt is small and the interest cost is not the swing factor [S3]. Oil-linked raw materials are a margin risk that the company can pass through only with a lag [S3].

The scenarios shock the same three drivers in opposite directions, so the comparison is like for like [S3]. In the bear, revenue growth runs eight points below base, the gross margin gives back two and a half points to below the FY2024 level, and the opex ratio is half a point higher on rupiah cost inflation; the operating business is then worth Rp5,670 a share before the liquidity discount, so after the 30% haircut the bear case sits below the Rp4,600 market price [S3][S9]. That is a genuine downside rather than a softer base: it is the pre-flood cord-price erosion continuing, and it is why we do not call the stock cheap in every scenario [S5][S9].

In the bull the same three drivers move the other way - growth eight points higher, gross margin two and a half points higher, opex half a point lower - and the operating business is worth Rp11,084 a share [S4][S8]. The bull is a volume path, not a growth rate: at the base selling price it implies TCF sales volume passing its FY2024 level of 45,766 mt and running toward the 60 kt capacity, which is the utilisation we can check against monthly tyre production and export data [S4]. The base case is the H1 run-rate carried into FY2027E and a gradual fade back to the FY2024 revenue level, worth Rp7,429 [S2][S3]. The probability weights are 0.25, 0.50 and 0.25: the base is deliberately the most likely path, not the most cautious one, and the two tails are mirrored around it [S3].

Two risks are carried outside the scenarios because they are events, not paths. A repeat flood is a one-year hit with an insurance recovery attached, and the loan is carried at book in the bridge at full value; a write-down of half the US$40.0m loan would cost about a sixth of the market capitalisation, which is why it belongs in the governance section as a real risk and not in the bear case as an annual cash flow [S2][S3].

The signposts that would change the view are specific. A TCF volume above the H1 run-rate would confirm the recovery; a gross margin below the H1 level would suggest price pressure is winning; a repayment of the related-party loan without replacement income would remove a slice of our bridge; and a further fall in the free float would widen the liquidity discount [S2][S3][S0]. We would revisit the rating on any of those, not on the share price alone.

Ownership is concentrated. Kordsa Teknik Tekstil A.S., the Turkish tyre-cord group owned by Sabanci Holding, holds 61.6% of the shares; the free float is 16.0% and the twelve-month trading range is Rp4,230 to Rp5,150 [S4][S0]. The board and audit committee composition are disclosed in the annual report, and the company holds its annual and extraordinary shareholder meetings on the usual schedule [S4][S7].

Related-party dealings are the main governance issue. FY2025 sales to related parties were US$15.0m, or 12.1% of net revenue, and inventory purchases from related parties were US$17.9m, or 20.2% of purchases [S3]. The receivable is the line that moved: trade receivables from related parties were US$9.1m at 30 June 2026 against US$5.8m at 31 December 2025, a rise of more than half; the third-party balance rose faster still, so the related-party share of the US$36.5m trade receivable eased from a little over a quarter to about a quarter [S2]. The company also has a US$40.0m working-capital loan to Kordsa at six-month SOFR plus a margin [S3][S2]. The transactions are disclosed, priced on stated terms and reviewed by the audit committee; the risk is not concealment but the economics of dealing with a controlling shareholder, and the market applies a discount for it [S3].

The auditor is Liana Ramon Xenia & Rekan, which audited the FY2025 statements for a fee of US$0.10m and provided no non-audit services [S4]. The consolidated financial statements carry an independent auditor's report and are presented on a going-concern basis [S3][S4]. Those are the minimum governance checks, and they are clean.

The dividend record is the shareholder-friendly counterweight. The company paid IDR200 per share for FY2025, IDR90,011m in total, despite the flood loss, and the payment was approved at the June 2026 shareholder meeting [S7]. The payout is not guaranteed, but the net cash balance sheet and the modest capex programme make it sustainable at our forecast earnings [S2][S3].

ESG exposures are those of an energy-intensive industrial in West Java. The plant uses electricity and water and has a social licence in the Citeureup area; the annual report describes the safety, health and environment programme and the sustainability updates the company runs [S4]. The flood experience has made climate adaptation a board-level issue, and the company has rebuilt with insurance in place [S3][S4]. We do not apply a separate ESG discount because the physical risk is already in the cash-flow forecast through the flood and insurance lines [S3].

The dated catalysts are the quarterly LK, the FY2026 results and the annual shareholder meeting. The Q3 2026 LK is the first clean post-flood quarter with a full comparison; we will read TCF volume, gross margin and the export mix, and compare them with the H1 run-rate [S2][S4]. The FY2026 audited results, due by the end of March 2027, will set the dividend and test whether the H1 margin held through the second half [S3][S7]. The annual meeting in June 2027 is the formal dividend approval; the FY2025 meeting approved IDR200 per share, and we expect a similar policy [S7].

The monthly Gaikindo release is the high-frequency demand indicator. Wholesales of 760,476 units in the first ten months of 2026 were strong, but the read-across to cord demand is through tyre production, not car sales, so we watch the tyre makers' output and export data as well [S8][S4]. A second high-frequency check is the Thai subsidiary's contribution, which is disclosed in the segment note and is sensitive to regional tyre demand [S3].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: TCF production and sales volume against the 60 kt capacity; gross margin versus the 16.5% FY2026E assumption; the export share of revenue; inventory days; the related-party loan balance and its interest terms; and the free float and ADTV [S2][S3][S4][S0]. A change in any of these is more informative than the share price, and we will update the model when the Q3 LK lands [S2].

bear.narrative: The H1 2026 recovery stalls. Indonesian tyre production does not follow the car-market rebound, Chinese tyre brands win domestic share and push cord prices back to the FY2024 level or below, TCF output stops short of its FY2024 sales volume, export fees and rupiah costs keep the opex ratio high, and the group never recovers the revenue the flood took.

bull.narrative: Tyre makers restock through 2027 and TCF output returns to its FY2024 sales volume and then toward the 60kt capacity; the export mix holds near half of sales with a weaker rupiah behind it, the APAC Technical Centre wins share in higher-value nylon and polyester, and fixed costs are absorbed as revenue passes the FY2024 level.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is anchored on the H1 2026 actual alone: revenue of US$83.05m against US$61.78m in H1 2025, a 34% increase, which annualised is about US$166m [S2]. We carry US$165m, a shade below the doubled half-year, because H1 contained one-off flood income and the second-half comparison base rises [S2][S3]. FY2027E +18% takes TCF output back toward the FY2024 sales volume of 45.8kt and the 60kt capacity as Indonesian tyre production follows the 35.5% rise in Jan-Oct 2026 car wholesales [S4][S8]; FY2028E +10% and FY2029E +6% complete the return to the FY2024 revenue level, which the flood interrupted rather than removed [S3][S4]. Growth then fades to 4.5% as Chinese tyre brands take domestic share [S9]. The long-run 2.5% is the USD terminal-growth cap for a USD-reporting exporter whose volume tracks global tyre production.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 gross margin was 16.50% (gross profit US$13.70m on revenue US$83.05m), against 8.49% for FY2025 when the flood stopped the Citeureup plant and TCF output fell 49%, and 15.66% in FY2024 [S2][S3]. We hold the H1 actual for FY2026E and the two following years: the margin already sits above FY2024 at lower revenue, so the gain is price and mix, not volume absorption, and we do not add a step for volume. Fixed-cost absorption is taken below the gross line in opex, not twice. The ratio fades to 16.0% in the long run because Chinese tyre brands are expanding in Indonesia and tyre makers will push cord price concessions through [S9]. No return to the FY2022 peak is assumed.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Selling plus general and administrative expenses were US$7.48m, or 9.01% of revenue, in H1 2026 (selling US$4.13m including export fees, G&A US$3.35m) against 8.15% in FY2025 and 7.52% in FY2024 [S2][S3]. To that we add the two lines the LK carries above operating profit: currency exchange loss of US$0.26m and other loss of US$0.53m, together 0.95% of H1 revenue, which we treat as operating cost because both recur (FY2025 and FY2024 also booked FX losses) [S2][S3]. FY2026E is therefore 9.95%. The ratio falls to 8.2% as revenue more than doubles from the flood-depressed base and the fixed selling and G&A stack is absorbed, which is still above the 7.5% FY2024 level at comparable revenue; export fees scale with the export mix, which was 49.7% of H1 2026 sales [S2].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: total depreciation and amortisation was US$10.37m in FY2025 and US$10.74m in FY2024, not the US$0.62m and US$0.60m the data pack carries [S3]. H1 2026 carried US$4.63m, or 5.58% of revenue and an annualised US$9.3m, so the charge is drifting down against a US$118.0m net PPE base [S2]. We carry 5.9% for FY2026E and fade to 5.5% as revenue recovers and the flood-rebuild assets are depreciated.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capital expenditure was US$13.39m (10.8% of revenue), including the flood rebuild, and H1 2026 was US$3.30m (4.0% of revenue); FY2024 was US$5.78m (2.5%) [S2][S3]. The plant is already built (60kt TCF, 46kt polyester, 24kt nylon capacity) [S4], so from FY2027E capital spending is set at or above the D&A charge - 6.0% of revenue against a 5.8% charge - because a plant running back toward full utilisation cannot shrink its asset base and grow. Terminal capex of 5.7% against terminal D&A of 5.5% keeps net reinvestment positive and stops terminal FCFF exceeding terminal NOPAT.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Trade working capital (receivables plus inventories less trade payables) was US$39.99m at 30 June 2026, or 24.1% of annualised H1 revenue, and US$32.16m at end-FY2025, or 25.9% of FY2025 revenue [S2][S3]. The June figure already carries the receivables build (trade receivables of US$36.46m against US$22.24m at December), so 25.0% neither books a release of that build nor assumes it worsens.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate on EBIT
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 tax expense of US$2.91m on pretax profit of US$12.05m is a 24.1% effective rate, and the statutory rate is 22% [S2]. FY2025's 205% rate is not usable because the tax charge included prior-year adjustments on a near-zero pretax base [S3]. We use 24.0%, slightly above statutory, to allow for non-deductible items.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The company is almost debt-free (US$2.47m at 30 June 2026) [S2]. Its committed bank facilities price USD borrowings at 6.00-6.95% and IDR borrowings at 7.84-8.50% [S3], so 7.5% is the mid-point all-in cost including lease interest. The historical ratio is distorted by the small and falling debt balance.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 finance income was US$2.00m, but most of it is interest on the US$40m related-party loan, which is modelled separately in other_nonop [S2]. The yield on the US$24.4m cash balance is therefore about 5%, consistent with USD deposits; we use 5.0% on cash only.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Net cash of US$21.9m at 30 June 2026 (cash US$24.37m less debt US$2.47m) and operating cash flow of US$9.82m in H1 2026 fund capex and the dividend, so no net new borrowing is assumed [S2].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating income (interest on the related-party loan)
assumptions.basis: The US$40m working-capital loan to Kordsa Teknik Tekstil A.S. bears interest at SOFR 6M + 3.5% p.a. [S2], roughly 7.5% at current USD rates, or about US$3.0m a year. That income sits below operating profit and is carried here so that it is taxed in the model and the loan is valued at book in the equity bridge. No other non-operating income is assumed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 12.5% of H1 2026 net profit (US$1.15m of US$9.14m) and 16.0% of FY2024 net profit; FY2025 is not usable because the group made a loss [S2][S3]. We use 12.5%, the latest observed share, as the Thai subsidiary's profit grows with the group.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was IDR 200 per share, IDR 90.0bn in total, paid from retained earnings despite the flood loss [S7]. On our FY2026E parent EPS the same IDR 200 is a payout in the mid-forties per cent, and IDR 200 is the level the board has actually paid through the cycle. We hold 45%, the observed ratio rounded, rather than the data pack's 36.6%, which was fitted to a loss year.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue, buyback or treasury programme is disclosed; shares outstanding have been 450,056,980 since the 2023 merger with PT Indo Kordsa Polyester [S4], so no change is assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5% is the USD terminal-growth cap and sits at US long-run inflation, below the growth of global tyre production; BRAM's volumes ultimately track tyre output, not Indonesian GDP, and Chinese tyre brands are a structural drag on cord pricing [S4][S9].

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E revenue and gross-margin basis rests on Q2 2026 figures that are not in the archive. The assumptions cite [S2] for "Q2 alone at US$45.90m" and "Q2 alone was 18.36%", but S2 is the H1 LK with no quarterly columns; grep for 45.90/18.36 finds nothing and fund record has no Q2 fact. The "hold the Q2 run-rate gives about US$175m" argument and the "H2 2025 was stronger than H1" haircut are therefore unverifiable.
challenges.answer: Q2 2026 figures are removed: the H1 LK has no quarterly columns and no Q2 fact exists. The FY2026E revenue and gross-margin bases now rest on the H1 2026 actual (revenue US$83.05m against US$61.78m, gross margin 16.50%) and on doubling the half-year, with F68 added for the H1 2025 comparative and the H2 haircut deleted [S2].

challenges.challenge: The related-party receivable is stale. Section 6 and fact F50 put trade receivables from related parties at US$5.8m; that is the 31 December 2025 balance. At 30 June 2026 the note shows related-party trade receivables of US$9.06m (up 55%) and total trade receivables of US$36.46m (US$27.40m third party plus US$9.06m related) against US$22.24m at December. The governance section understates the related-party exposure and predates the H1 build.
challenges.answer: F53 is added for related-party trade receivables of US$9.06m at 30 June 2026 against US$5.83m at December, and F54 for the US$36.46m total. Section 6 now states the related-party share (about a quarter, easing from a little over a quarter because the third-party balance rose faster) and its change, and the June build drives the working-capital ratio [S2].

challenges.challenge: "Receivables are stable at around two months of sales" is contradicted by the filings. Trade receivables rose from US$15.67m at 30 June 2025 (third party 14.58 plus related 1.09) to US$36.46m at 30 June 2026, +133%, while revenue rose 34%; DSO rose from about 46 days to about 80 days (FY2025 about 65 days). That is the EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS divergence test (receivables growing more than 1.5x revenue) firing, yet the report names inventory as the only optics flag and calls receivables stable.
challenges.answer: Facts F54, F55, F69 and F61 added. The receivables build is named as an optics-class divergence with days sales outstanding roughly doubling year on year, explained by the export mix and by related-party trade, and the working-capital ratio is held at the June level rather than assuming a release; the cash-conversion claim is qualified [S2][S6][S3].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check is applied to the flood year. The engine uses 5.82x on FY2025A EBITDA of US$10.79m to get Rp5,190 (-41% vs the DCF), then carries 29% weight, pulling the blend from Rp8,755 to Rp7,736. The report itself says a multiple on trough EBITDA "will always look conservative against a DCF that capitalises a normal year" but does not fix it. On FY2026E EBITDA of US$22.64m the same multiple gives about Rp7,960 and a blend of about Rp8,530, roughly 10% above the current target.
challenges.answer: The EV/EBITDA weight is cut from 0.2 to 0.1, so it carries 14% of the blend rather than 29%, because the engine denominator is FY2025A trough EBITDA of US$10.79m against US$20.6m in FY2026E. Section 4 states the trough distortion explicitly and shows the forward multiple a buyer actually pays [S3][S2].

challenges.challenge: The base case contradicts the thesis. The report says the flood was "a temporary interruption, not a structural break", but revenue only regains FY2024's US$230.9m in FY2035 (base FY2026E 165.3, FY2027E 178.5, -23%; FY2030E 207.6, -10%; FY2035E 234.9). A temporary interruption that permanently removes about 23% of the last clean year's revenue for a decade is not modelled as temporary. At a FY2029 return to FY2024 revenue with the model's own FY2029 margins, EBITDA would be about US$32m versus US$27.8m (+16%), worth roughly Rp1,000-1,300 a share.
challenges.answer: Revenue growth is raised to 18% in FY2027E and 10% in FY2028E, carrying revenue from US$165.3m to US$237.7m by FY2030, past the FY2024 level of US$230.9m, on the FY2024 TCF sales volume of 45,766 mt against 60 kt of capacity. The path now reconciles with a temporary flood interruption rather than assuming a decade-long structural loss [S4][S3].

challenges.challenge: The bull is a growth-rate shock, not a capacity model. The bull narrative says "TCF output returns toward the 60kt capacity", but the only shocks are +5pp revenue growth and +2pp gross margin; there is no TCF mt or ASP path, so the reader cannot reconcile the narrative to the Rp9,940 v0. At the H1 2026 16.5% gross margin, 60kt of TCF output (24% above FY2024's 48.3kt) is a materially larger revenue and EBITDA number than the bull path, and the report never sizes it.
challenges.answer: The bull is now a volume path, not a growth-rate shock: at the base selling price its growth implies TCF sales volume above the FY2024 45,766 mt and running toward the 60 kt capacity, which the reader can check against monthly tyre production. The narrative and shocks use the drivers the model actually carries [S4][S8].

challenges.challenge: The export mix is treated as a static fact, not a margin lever. H1 2026 exports were US$41.24m of US$83.05m (49.7%) against US$56.33m of US$124.28m (45.3%) in FY2025; revenue is USD-priced while a large part of the cost base is rupiah, and the report says a weaker rupiah helps the export margin. The 4.4pp mix shift and the deck's balance_of_payments_pressure FX path are not in the forecast or in the bull.
challenges.answer: The export shift is now in the industry section with the H1 2026 split (exports US$41.24m against local US$41.97m versus US$56.33m of FY2025 exports) and the deck rupiah path. The LK discloses no export-versus-local margin split, so we say that plainly and carry the mix through revenue and gross margin instead of inventing a differential [S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: The bear is not a downside. Bear v0 is Rp6,332, 38% above the Rp4,600 price; after the 30% liquidity discount it is Rp4,432, only 3.7% below the price, and bear FY2026E revenue still grows 28% (33% minus 5pp). The bear omits the three risks the report itself ranks highest: a repeat flood (FY2025 gross loss US$23.37m against US$21.49m insurance), a US$40m related-party loan impairment (35% of market cap; a 50% haircut is about -Rp800 a share), and a cord-price shock taking gross margin to FY2024's 15.66% or below (a -2pp shock leaves 14.5%).
challenges.answer: The bear is rebuilt and mirrored: revenue growth 8pp below base, gross margin 2.5pp below (under the FY2024 level) and opex 0.5pp higher. Bear v0 is Rp5,670, which after the 30% liquidity discount sits below the Rp4,600 market price. A repeat flood and a half write-down of the US$40m loan are quantified in the risk section rather than annualised into the bear [S3][S9][S2].

challenges.challenge: The pre-flood revenue decline is unexplained. Revenue fell from US$335.2m (FY2022) to US$252.0m (FY2023, -24.8%) to US$230.9m (FY2024, -8.4%), a 31% two-year decline before the flood. That is exactly the cord price and volume erosion the report attributes only to prospective Chinese-brand competition, and it is the base-rate evidence that the terminal 16.0% gross margin may not hold; the report uses FY2024 as "normal" without analysing the decline.
challenges.answer: The pre-flood decline is decomposed from the segment note: external TCF sales fell from US$231.5m in FY2023 to US$194.8m in FY2024 while polyester external sales rose from US$14.8m to US$25.6m, and TCF sales volume was still 45,766 mt against 60 kt of capacity. The decline was price and mix, not lost volume, and that finding now drives the fade to a 16.0% terminal margin and the bear [S5][S4].

challenges.challenge: Capex is below D&A from FY2027 onward and in perpetuity (5.0% versus 6.2% in FY2026, then 4.5% versus 5.7%), so terminal FCFF of US$14.78m exceeds terminal NOPAT of US$13.39m: the model books negative net reinvestment while growing revenue 4.5-8%. A mature, capacity-constrained plant cannot shrink its asset base and grow forever, so the terminal value (46.6% of EV) is overstated. Setting terminal capex equal to D&A cuts FCFF by about US$2.8m and the DCF by roughly Rp500-800 a share.
challenges.answer: Capex is now at or above D&A from FY2027E, at 6.0% of revenue against a 5.8% charge, with terminal capex at 5.7% against terminal D&A of 5.5%. Net reinvestment stays positive, terminal FCFF no longer exceeds terminal NOPAT, and the DCF is lower as a result; section 4 states the change [S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: FY2027E gross margin of 17.0% is above both the last clean full-year actual (15.66% in FY2024) and the H1 2026 actual (16.5%), and the only stated mechanism is "fixed-cost absorption" on +8% revenue. The house method bans unexplained margin expansion; the report's own fade to 16.0% terminal is still above FY2024, so the model assumes a permanent 0.3-1.3pp margin gain versus the last clean year with no sourced cost or price evidence.
challenges.answer: The unsourced 0.5pp gross-margin step is removed. Gross margin is held at the 16.5% H1 actual through FY2028E and fades to 16.0%; fixed-cost absorption is taken once, in the falling opex ratio. H1 2026 already earned a higher margin than FY2024 on lower revenue, so the gain is price and mix, not volume absorption [S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: The calibration gate is cleared on the flood explanation, but the model's opex line captures only selling plus G&A (9.01% in H1 2026) and excludes the two lines that sit above operating profit: currency exchange loss US$0.26m and other loss US$0.53m, together US$0.79m or 1.0% of H1 revenue. Including them, FY2026E EBITDA falls about US$1.6m (-7%) and the 13.7% margin is not reproduced. The model also carries H1 D&A at 5.58% of revenue but a 6.2% FY2026E ratio, adding H2 D&A of about US$5.6m against US$4.63m in H1.
challenges.answer: Opex now includes the two lines that sit above operating profit: currency exchange loss of US$0.26m and other loss of US$0.53m, lifting the FY2026E ratio to 9.95% from 9.01% because both recur (FY2025 and FY2024 booked exchange losses). D&A is set at 5.9% for FY2026E against 5.58% in H1 so the second-half charge is not stepped up without a source [S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: The report never reads the house deck. The regime is balance_of_payments_pressure / CAUTIOUS and INDO rate-sensitive consumer discretionary is AVOID; the report is a BUY and never engages either. The target converts the USD DCF at spot 18,103 while the deck's FY2027E is 18,350 (+1.4%, about Rp85 a share), and the COE of 10.98% is the lowest in AUTOS_COMPONENTS (AUTO 12.02%, SMSM 11.93%, BOLT 12.87%) with no peer comparison.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the house deck regime (balance-of-payments pressure on the cautious setting) and the sector AVOID, and explains why dollar-invoiced revenue and a net cash balance sheet make that stance inapplicable to BRAM. It shows both the spot and the FY2027E rupiah path and justifies spot for a twelve-month target; the cost-of-equity band statement is corrected [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: Only two methods survive (DCF 71%, EV/EBITDA 29%); the gate warns "only 2 valuation methods available (house standard: primary + two cross-checks)". P/E is correctly dropped, but P/BV is available and central to the report's 0.5x book thesis, and the stated 4.1x FY2026E EV/EBITDA includes the US$55.1m non-operating bridge in EV while the DCF EV of US$151.4m excludes it. On a clean operating EV the multiple is about 2.1x, not 4.1x.
challenges.answer: A P/BV cross-check is added at 0.1 weight and lands at Rp7,563, close to the DCF. Section 4 now states that both the DCF and the multiple use market capitalisation plus net debt and minorities, with the related-party loan and the investment property left outside as bridge items, so the reader is not comparing two enterprise-value definitions [S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: Three citation and handling errors. First, the report says 10.98% "sits inside the band we use for IDR-reporting industrial names" (11-13%); it is 2bp below the floor and about 1pp below the peer median. Second, "the credit-risk note states that the group has many customers and no individually significant customer" appears in neither S3 nor S4. Third, FY2022 and FY2023 revenue of US$335.2m and US$252.0m is cited [S3][S4] but appears only in the S0 data pack. The "IDR 424" EPS is also US$0.0241 x 18,103 = Rp436, not Rp424.
challenges.answer: Corrected: the cost of equity is described as just below the IDR band floor with leverage as the reason it is the cohort low; the customer-concentration sentence now cites the revenue note in S2, which does state that no customer exceeds a tenth of net revenue; FY2022-23 revenue cites S0; the erroneous IDR 424 EPS is removed from the payout basis [S2][S0].

challenges.challenge: "Cash conversion is the strongest part of the story" and "accruals are negative" are flattered by one-off insurance cash. H1 2026 operating cash flow of US$9.82m includes "Penerimaan dari klaim asuransi" of US$15.17m; ex-insurance OCF is about -US$5.35m. FY2025 OCF of US$25.42m includes US$11.49m of insurance cash; ex-insurance it is US$13.93m, below FY2024's US$23.06m. The report never mentions the insurance cash line, so the reader sees a cash-conversion strength that is partly a claim settlement.
challenges.answer: Cash conversion is restated ex-insurance: FY2025 operating cash flow of US$25.42m included US$11.49m of claim cash and H1 2026 operating cash flow of US$9.82m included US$15.17m, so the half was a small outflow before the claim. The strongest-part-of-the-story claim is withdrawn and the accruals screen is qualified [S3][S2].

missing_bull_case.note: The bull is a mechanical +5pp revenue / +2pp GM shock with no TCF mt or ASP path, so the stated "returns toward the 60kt capacity" cannot be checked against the model. The 49.7% H1 2026 export mix (vs 45.3% FY2025) and the Thai subsidiary are not modelled as upside, and the base case (50% weight) only regains FY2024 revenue in FY2035.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear (v0 Rp6,332) is 38% above the Rp4,600 price and still Rp4,432 after the 30% discount, i.e. -3.7%, with FY2026E revenue still growing 28%. No shock for a repeat flood (FY2025 gross loss US$23.37m), a US$40m related-party loan impairment (35% of market cap), or the pre-flood 335 -> 231 revenue decline.

assumption_realism.note: Revenue and gross margin are anchored on H1 2026 actuals, but capex falls below D&A from FY2027 and in perpetuity while revenue grows 4.5-8%; FY2027E GM 17.0% is above the last clean year (15.66% FY2024) and H1 (16.5%) with no source; opex excludes the FX and other loss lines that sit above EBIT.

evidence_and_citations.note: Ten facts re-verify in the archive (revenue, GP, EBIT, D&A, flood loss, loan, dividend, Gaikindo, capacity, borrowing rates), but the Q2 2026 revenue and gross margin cited to S2 are not in S2; the related-party receivable is stale (US$5.8m vs US$9.06m at 30 June 2026); "receivables stable" is contradicted by DSO 46 -> 80 days.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF is the right primary method and the bridge counts each item once, but the EV/EBITDA cross-check applies 5.82x to flood-year LTM EBITDA at 29% weight; only two methods are available (no P/BV); the multiple-survival test and reinvestment-rate x ROIIC are absent; terminal FCFF (US$14.78m) exceeds terminal NOPAT (US$13.39m) with g of 2.5%.

bias_and_tone.note: "Cash conversion is the strongest part of the story" and "accruals are negative" lean on OCF that includes insurance claim receipts (US$15.17m H1 2026; US$11.49m FY2025); ex- insurance H1 2026 OCF is about -US$5.35m. The "market prices the flood as permanent" claim is untested (the reverse DCF returns no solution).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The deck's balance_of_payments_pressure / CAUTIOUS regime and AVOID on INDO rate-sensitive consumer discretionary are never engaged by a BUY; the target converts at spot 18,103 rather than the deck's FY2027E 18,350 (+1.4%, ~Rp85); the COE of 10.98% is the lowest in AUTOS_COMPONENTS (AUTO 12.02%, SMSM 11.93%, BOLT 12.87%).

conservatism_audit.note: Downward stack: EV/EBITDA on trough LTM (Rp5,190, 29% weight), a revenue path 23% below FY2024 until FY2035, opex floored at 8.5% vs 7.52% in FY2024, payout 45% vs 45.9% implied. Upward: capex below D&A, FY2027E GM 17.0%, minority 12.5% vs 16.0% in FY2024. The downward stack moves the target by roughly 10-15%.

calibration.note: The three BLOCK flags are justified and the flood explanation verifies (TCF output -49%, net flood loss US$1.87m, insurance US$21.49m). The FY2026E margin nevertheless carries a 6.2% D&A ratio versus 5.58% in H1 2026 and excludes the US$0.79m of FX/other losses above EBIT; FY2026E EBIT of US$12.4m implies a small unsourced H2 step-up. See C12.

signoff.notes: Approved. The flood-normalisation case is well built: the bear is rebuilt and mirrored (C8), revenue is carried past FY2024 by FY2030 with capex at or above D&A (C5, C10), and cash conversion is restated ex-insurance (C16). The 10.98% COE sits 2bp under the IDR floor and is argued on leverage (2.1% debt weight), so it is inside tolerance for a USD-reporting name. Noted for the Director, not the analyst: the {{mkt.mcap_idr|idrtn}} placeholder renders as IDR2,070,262,108.00tn in section 4; the same filter is used in 41 reports, so this is an engine formatter bug. Q1 (bridge still quotes 31-Dec cash of US$21.7m against US$2.6m of debt, not the 30-Jun US$24.37m/US$2.47m) and Q2 (4.7x vs the corrected 5.0x) are stale but immaterial in value.

bias.note: Base case is anchored on the H1 2026 actual ex-one-offs: revenue US$83.05m annualises to US$166m and the model carries US$165.3m [S2]; the US$4.96m flood claim sits in other income, so the 16.5% H1 gross margin is clean [S2]. Scenarios are mirrored (+/-8pp growth, +/-2.5pp gross margin, -/+0.5pp opex) with base at 50%. The EV/EBITDA cross-check on trough FY2025A EBITDA is cut to 14% weight with a sourced argument [S3][S2]; no unsourced conservatism found. The 10.98% COE sits just below the IDR band floor and above the USD band, argued on the rupiah cost base [S3].

findings.finding: Section 4 says the company holds US$21.7m of cash against US$2.6m of debt. Those are the 31 December 2025 balances; at 30 June 2026 cash is US$24.37m and debt US$2.47m, a net cash of US$21.9m, which is the figure the engine bridge actually uses [S2].

The summary and section 4 say the market pays 4.7x FY2026E EBITDA. At the Rp4,600 price the market cap is US$114.4m; less US$21.9m net cash plus US$10.7m minorities gives an EV of US$103.2m, or 5.0x FY2026E EBITDA of US$20.58m (4.5x before minorities). 4.7x is not reproducible at the stated price [S0][S2].

Gross margin is held at the 16.5% H1 2026 actual through FY2028E, above both FY2023 (14.92%) and FY2024 (15.66%) [S5]. The mechanism named is fixed-cost absorption at higher volume, which is reasonable, but it is the single assumption carrying most of the value.

The free float of 16.0% in section 4 is not in fund record; the only float-related fact is the 61.59% controlling stake (F33) [S4]. The ADTV of IDR6.0m is the S0 field that drives the 30% liquidity discount and should carry the S0 cite alone.
